lesson.title: Confrontation in Birmingham: Fire Hoses, Police Dogs, and a Letter from Jail
lesson.summary: In the spring of 1963, the SCLC's campaign to desegregate Birmingham, Alabama, one of the South's most rigidly segregated cities, produced images of police violence against nonviolent protesters, including children, that shocked the nation and built irresistible momentum for federal civil rights action.
lesson.body:
By 1963, Birmingham, Alabama, was widely regarded as one of the most thoroughly segregated cities in the country, and one of the most violent: so many racially motivated bombings had targeted Black homes, businesses, and churches over the preceding years that some residents grimly nicknamed it Bombingham. The Reverend Fred Shuttlesworth, whose own home and church had both been bombed for his civil rights activism, led a local organization called the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights and invited Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference to bring a major campaign to the city, believing that Birmingham's extreme resistance to change made it a place where progress there could reshape the entire nation's view of segregation.

The campaign, organized under the internal codename Project C, for confrontation, combined sit ins, marches, and a boycott of downtown businesses during the Easter shopping season to pressure local merchants and officials to desegregate. King was arrested on April 12, 1963, Good Friday, along with dozens of other demonstrators, and it was during this stay in the Birmingham city jail that he wrote what became known as the Letter from Birmingham Jail, a lengthy response to a group of white Alabama clergymen who had publicly urged that the protests were unwise and untimely. King's letter argued that justice delayed indefinitely was justice denied, and that nonviolent direct action was necessary precisely because voluntary change had not come and would not come without pressure.

As the campaign continued, organizers faced a practical problem: many adults in Birmingham's Black community, fearing the loss of jobs or worse, were reluctant to risk arrest by marching. In early May 1963, organizers turned to Birmingham's young people instead, and in what became known as the Children's Crusade, hundreds and eventually thousands of schoolchildren, some quite young, walked out of school to march downtown in disciplined, nonviolent lines. Commissioner of Public Safety Eugene Bull Connor responded by ordering police and firefighters to turn high pressure fire hoses, powerful enough to knock people off their feet and tear bark from trees, directly on the young marchers, and to use police dogs against them, while officers arrested marchers by the hundreds until the city's jails overflowed.

Photographs and television footage of police dogs lunging at teenagers and fire hoses battering children in the street were published and broadcast nationally and internationally within days, producing a wave of public horror and outrage that reshaped how many Americans, and much of the world, understood the reality of segregation. That pressure, combined with the economic toll of the boycott, pushed local business leaders to negotiate, and by early May they agreed to desegregate some public facilities and expand hiring for Black employees. The agreement did not end the violence: white extremists bombed the motel where King had been staying and the home of his brother, A. D. King, within days of the settlement, and that September a bomb planted at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church in Birmingham killed four young girls, Addie Mae Collins, Cynthia Wesley, Carole Robertson, and Denise McNair, a horrifying reminder of the violence the movement still faced. What Birmingham demonstrated beyond the city itself was the power of nonviolent confrontation to expose that violence to a national audience, building pressure on the Kennedy administration and Congress that would shape the civil rights battles still to come.
